source.title_on_document: Homogenization Effects of Large Language Models on Human Creative Ideation

supplement.where: No separate supplementary material or online appendix is referenced in the document. The ordinary in-document Appendix A, Validating Sentence Embeddings for Homogenization Analysis, is included on PDF pp. 12-13 (printed pp. 424-425); Section 4.1.1 on PDF p. 5 points to it.
supplement.holds: The in-document Appendix A explains embedding validation against human-coded idea categories and reports agreement percentages in Table 2. It adds no participant sample or AI-condition contrast. The AI-condition outcome statistics are in the main text (PDF pp. 5-7); no separately printed standard errors or external supplementary statistics are identified.

paper_design_summary: In a within-subjects user study, 36 adults were recruited and 33 were analyzed; each participant answered four 8-minute divergent-thinking prompts based on the Torrance Tests, two with ChatGPT 3.5 and two with a web version of the non-AI Oblique Strategies card deck, with tool and prompt order randomized per participant and balanced (PDF pp. 3-4, Sections 3.1-3.3). The paper reports 1271 ideas in total and scores the outputs for group-level and individual-level semantic divergence, fluency, flexibility, elaboration, and originality (PDF pp. 5-6, Sections 4.1 and 4.3). Participants also rated their responsibility for the ideas and completed the Creativity Support Index.

studies.label: Within-subjects user study: ChatGPT vs Oblique Strategies deck on four TTCT-style ideation prompts

assignment.what_was_assigned: Order of the two creativity support tools (ChatGPT, Oblique Strategies deck) and of the ideation prompts, per participant; every participant used both tools, two prompts with each
assignment.quote: The order of CSTs and prompts was randomized per participant and balanced across the entire experiment.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 416), Section 3.3 Procedure; design named on PDF p. 3 (printed p. 415), Section 3 ('We conducted a within-subjects experiment')

arms.name: ChatGPT
arms.description: Two ideation prompts (one Product Improvement, one Improbable Consequences) answered while free to use ChatGPT 3.5 (May 3, 2023 release for 6 participants, August 3, 2023 release for 30)

arms.name: Oblique Strategies (OS) deck
arms.description: The other two ideation prompts answered while using a web app version of the Oblique Strategies card deck, a non-AI creativity support tool whose cards carry prompts such as 'Turn it upside down'; the paper's control condition

participants.exclusions: Of 36 people originally recruited, 3 were excluded from all analyses for failure to follow directions (e.g., not using ChatGPT when prompted), leaving 33 people analyzed (PDF pp. 3-4, Sections 3.1.1-3.1.2). The paper does not separately state the count at random assignment, so n_randomized is null. Both tool conditions include the same 33 analyzed people. The CSI degrees of freedom and several process statistics are not reconciled with these exclusions (PDF p. 7, Sections 4.4.2-4.5.3).
participants.who: Adults aged 22 to 44 (M = 28.36) recruited from academic mailing lists, forums, and social media; the analyzed sample had 12 students, 10 creative professionals, and 11 other professionals; one-hour sessions remote-moderated over videoconference; $17.50 gift card
participants.quote: Of the 36 participants originally recruited, three were excluded from all analyses for failure to follow direction (e.g., not using ChatGPT when prompted to do so).
participants.locator: PDF p. 3 (printed p. 415), Section 3.1.1; PDF p. 4 (printed p. 416), Section 3.1.2 ('Our sample included 33 participants')

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT 3.5 (versions released May 3, 2023, n = 6, and August 3, 2023, n = 30)
ai_tool.how_used: Participants used ChatGPT freely while listing ideas. Most (86.11%, n = 31) pasted the ideation prompt into ChatGPT, and most (72.22%, n = 26) iterated on their prompt. 41.67% (n = 15) copied output directly, all but one selectively; 16.67% (n = 6) only paraphrased or drew inspiration; 38.89% (n = 14) combined both (PDF p. 7, printed p. 419, Sections 4.5.2-4.5.3). The paper does not explain how these process statistics relate to the exclusions.

task.description: Four prompts from two Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking task types: Product Improvement (make a stuffed toy animal more fun to play with; make a jigsaw puzzle more interesting) and Improbable Consequences (a great fog leaves only people's feet visible; gravity becomes very weak). For each prompt, participants listed as many ideas as possible and tried to think of ideas no one else would.
task.duration: 8 minutes per prompt, two prompts per tool (four prompts in total), within a one-hour remote-moderated session

outcomes.name: Group-level divergence (homogenization): divergence of each idea from the average embedding of all participant ideas for that task
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Cosine-similarity-based divergence of each idea from the average embedding of all participant ideas for the same prompt, plotted as Divergence (From Others), where higher means more distinct from the group (PDF p. 5, Sections 4.1.1-4.1.2 and Figure 2). Sentence embeddings use all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (SentenceTransformers); Appendix A reports 58.92% average agreement with human-coded idea categories (PDF p. 13, Table 2). The analyzed sample is 33 people and the reported test is t(32); the exact aggregation of idea-level scores into participant/tool scores is not stated.

contrasts.reported: ChatGPT (M = .24, SD = .07) vs OS (M = .28, SD = .08), t(32) = 2.154, p = 0.038, d = .47, 95% CI [.00,.07]. The measure is divergence (higher = more diverse), so no sign reversal is needed: ChatGPT ideas were less diverse across people (more homogeneous).
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 417), Section 4.1.2 and Figure 2

diversity_detail.metric: Semantic divergence of each idea from the average embedding of all participant ideas for the same prompt, based on cosine similarity; higher means more distinct from the group. The formula converting similarity to divergence and the exact aggregation of idea-level scores are not stated (PDF p. 5, Sections 4.1.1-4.1.2).
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each idea against the average embedding of all participant ideas for that prompt. The paper does not explicitly state whether this reference pools both tool conditions, excludes the scored idea, or how scores are aggregated for each participant and tool. Appendix A describes leave-one-out category embeddings for model validation, which does not establish the reference used for the primary homogenization analysis.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: t-test with 32 degrees of freedom on 33 participants' scores (the df match a paired test; the paper does not name the test), with a 95% CI; figure error bars are 95% CIs with Cousineau-Morey correction for within-subjects data.
diversity_detail.notes: Sign: the paper reports divergence, so lower = more homogeneous; ChatGPT's lower value means less diversity across people. The paper frames this as RQ1, and Appendix A calls the embedding analysis its 'primary homogenization analysis' (PDF p. 12, printed p. 424). The printed d is unsigned and its standardizer is not stated.

outcomes.name: Individual-level divergence: divergence of each idea from the average embedding of the same participant's other ideas for that prompt
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: The same all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embedding approach as S1-O1, but against the average embedding of the participant's other ideas for the same prompt, plotted as Divergence (From Self). It measures variety within one person's ideas, so it is coded flexibility (codebook Section 6). Section 4.1.3 prints means of .65 (ChatGPT) and .66 (OS), but Figure 3 plots lower values with the opposite ordering of the two means. The figure prints no numerical arm means; no values estimated from the chart are recorded. The text statistics are retained as printed pending clarification (PDF p. 5, Section 4.1.3 and Figure 3).

contrasts.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 417), Section 4.1.3 and Figure 3

outcomes.name: Fluency: number of ideas
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Simple count of ideas per participant with each tool; the paper describes about one additional idea, approximately a 15% increase, with ChatGPT. The paper does not state whether the count is per prompt or summed over the two prompts per tool.

contrasts.locator: PDF pp. 5-6 (printed pp. 417-418), Section 4.3.1 and Figure 5

outcomes.name: Flexibility: number of idea categories hit (hand-coded)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Iterative grounded-theory coding produced 181 idea categories from 1271 responses; each participant's responses were tagged with all relevant categories, and the outcome is the count of categories hit by each participant. Coders were blind to tool condition.

contrasts.locator: PDF p. 6 (printed p. 418), Section 4.3.2 and Figure 6

outcomes.name: Elaboration: stoplisted word count
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of the words used to express each idea, excluding a stoplist of common low-information filler words (method of Dumas et al. 2021, ref. [27]); a computed text-mining measure. No codebook measure code fits exactly; automated_score is the closest. The printed p = 0.237 conflicts with t(32) = 2.32 and with the 95% CI [.22,3.37], which excludes zero; p is recorded as printed.

contrasts.reported: ChatGPT (M = 8.25, SD = 4.61) vs OS (M = 6.46, SD = 2.55), t(32) = 2.32, p = 0.237, d = .48, 95% CI [.22,3.37] (p as printed; it conflicts with the t-statistic and the CI)
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 6 (printed p. 418), Section 4.3.3 and Figure 7

outcomes.name: Originality: number of unique ideas (ideas no other participant generated)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of a participant's ideas that no other participant also generated, a subcount from the hand-coded categories of Section 4.3.2. Robustness variants, which the paper says did not change the finding (PDF p. 6, Section 4.3.4): (a) unique responses at a 5% threshold (idea categories produced by less than 5% of participants): ChatGPT (M = .87, SD = .88) vs OS (M = .90, SD = 1.07), t(32) = .134, p = 0.894, d = .02, 95% CI [-.34,.39]; (b) weighted flexibility score (each category weighted by its frequency in the whole sample): ChatGPT (M = 6.34, SD = 3.31) vs OS (M = 5.50, SD = 3.01), t(32) = 1.424, p = 0.164, d = .26, 95% CI [-.35,2.02].

contrasts.reported: Unique ideas: ChatGPT (M = .74, SD = .69) vs OS (M = .97, SD = 1.00), t(32) = 1.65, p = 0.108, d = .26, 95% CI [-.05,.50]. Robustness variants are in measure_detail.

eligibility.reason: Randomized within-person order of ChatGPT and a non-AI Oblique Strategies tool meets criterion 1 (PDF p. 4, Section 3.3). The participant-produced ideas receive computed semantic-divergence scores and idea/category/word-count measures, meeting criterion 3 (PDF pp. 5-6, Sections 4.1.1-4.1.3 and 4.3). Only 33 people were analyzed after 3 exclusions from 36 recruited people (PDF pp. 3-4, Sections 3.1.1-3.1.2), so criterion 2 is not met; the same people used both tools and must not be counted twice. The random-assignment count is not separately stated. This randomized experiment belongs in the screening report as below the 50-person threshold, with context_class none. Remaining reporting and measurement uncertainties do not affect these decisions.

one_line_finding: Among 33 analyzed people, ChatGPT yielded lower group-level idea divergence than the Oblique Strategies deck (M = .24 vs .28, t(32) = 2.154, p = 0.038, d = .47; PDF p. 5, Section 4.1.2), with no clear difference in individual-level divergence (Section 4.1.3).
open_questions: Individual-level divergence (S1-O2): Section 4.1.3 prints M = .65 (ChatGPT) and .66 (OS), while Figure 3 plots lower values with the opposite ordering of the means (PDF p. 5). The paper does not establish whether the text reports similarity instead of divergence. No numerical values estimated from Figure 3 are retained; the text statistics remain as printed.

Elaboration (S1-O5): p = 0.237 is printed alongside t(32) = 2.32 and 95% CI [.22,3.37] (PDF p. 6, Section 4.3.3). These statistics are internally inconsistent; the form retains the printed values pending clarification.

Participant counts across analyses: the paper states 33 analyzed people and the output tests report t(32), but the CSI test reports t(35) and several process counts/percentages differ from the analyzed sample; the ChatGPT release counts are 6 and 30 (PDF pp. 3-4, Sections 3.1.1-3.2.1; PDF p. 7, Sections 4.4.2-4.5.3). The paper does not explain whether excluded participants enter the process and self-report results.

Group-level divergence computation (S1-O1): the text refers to all ideas generated for that task but does not explicitly define pooling across tools, exclusion of the scored idea, the similarity-to-divergence transformation, or aggregation into participant/tool scores (PDF p. 5, Sections 4.1.1-4.1.2). Appendix A's leave-one-out rule concerns category embeddings for model validation and does not settle these details of the main analysis.
Fluency (S1-O3): the means 8.39 (ChatGPT) and 7.32 (OS) are not explicitly labeled as per prompt or as summed over the two prompts per tool (PDF pp. 5-6, Section 4.3.1 and Figure 5).

Inferential conventions: the direction of the printed 95% CIs, the sign/standardizer of the reported d values, and the exact t-test specification are not stated (PDF pp. 5-6, Sections 4.1.2-4.3.4). The within-subjects design and reported degrees of freedom are recorded without assigning an unstated analysis formula.

Count at random assignment: the paper explicitly gives 36 recruited and 33 analyzed people, but no separate count at assignment (PDF pp. 3-4, Sections 3.1.1-3.3). Participant and arm n_randomized fields are null; the explicit randomization of tool order remains established.

Document identity and sample overlap: candidates.json names the CHI EA paper Evaluating Creativity Support Tools via Homogenization Analysis, while the saved PDF is the C&C paper Homogenization Effects of Large Language Models on Human Creative Ideation (PDF p. 1). The saved PDF does not confirm shared participants with the CHI EA paper. This screening applies to the saved C&C document; confirmation is needed before linking the samples.
notes: Self-reported measures are not listed as outcomes (form B listed them as S1-O7 and S1-O8): sense of responsibility, ChatGPT (M = 48.17%, SD = 26.22%) vs OS (M = 63.63%, SD = 17.36%), t(32) = 3.21, p = 0.003, d = .67, 95% CI [-24.60%, -5.51%,] (PDF p. 5, Section 4.2, Figure 4); Creativity Support Index, ChatGPT (M = 78.03%, SD = 18.82%) vs OS (M = 73.98%, SD = 15.35 %), t(35) = 1.028, p = 0.312, d = .24, 95% CI [-3.94%, 12.02%], with no differences on any subscale (PDF p. 7, Section 4.4.2). Section 4.5.4 (PDF p. 7) reports non-randomized comparisons within the ChatGPT condition (own ideas first vs LLM first; creative vs copied prompt) and correlations of the number of prompts entered with the number of ideas (r(32)=.43, p = .008), weighted uniqueness (r(32)=.46, p = .004), and homogeneity (r(32)=.23, p = .185); these are not randomized contrasts and are not listed. Table 1 (PDF p. 7) reports interview themes, not scored outcomes. The paper did not rate idea quality and used no human creativity ratings (Section 4.3). Participants who used ChatGPT first produced their OS ideas afterward; the paper reports no results by order. Design class: sessions were remote-moderated over videoconference (Section 3.3) and the authors describe a 'lab context' (Section 6), so lab_rct. Outcome ids follow the paper's section order, as in form A; form B numbered flexibility S1-O3 and fluency S1-O4. Final review read the complete current markdown conversion, including references and Appendix A, and verified the recorded statistics on the PDF pages. Appendix A validates embeddings on the same idea dataset and adds no separate human experiment. No c001 challenge files were present; the final challenge counts are therefore zero. Final spec/evidence corrections set inferred randomized counts to null, distinguish an unstated external supplement from the included Appendix A, remove numerical estimates read from Figure 3, and qualify unstated aggregation details. The reconciliation object is preserved unchanged as the historical reconciliation; its inferred randomized count is superseded by the final fields. The candidate record identifies a different title/DOI from the saved C&C document; no unverified shared-sample claim is added.

Samples for process and self-report analyses: authors must explain which excluded participants, if any, enter those analyses; the output sample remains below 50 people.

S1-O1 computation: authors must specify the reference pool, self-exclusion rule, similarity-to-divergence transformation, and participant/tool aggregation; the outcome is already confirmed as scored on output.
S1-O3 fluency denominator: authors must state whether the reported score is per prompt or aggregated across prompts; this does not change the participant count or output criterion.
Inferential conventions: authors must specify CI contrast direction, d standardizer/sign, and t-test form; none changes the three eligibility findings.
Count at assignment: authors could provide the number assigned an order; the randomized-order procedure and the analyzed count already settle criteria 1 and 2.
CHI EA/C&C sample linkage: authors must confirm whether the documents share participants before deduplication; the saved C&C experiment remains below 50 analyzed people.
